title: Marguerite and the Glasshouse
premise: Wendell Dunmore, a translator raised bilingual in a dying dialect her mother called 'the glasshouse language'—beautiful, enclosed, and meant to keep things in—returns to her estranged family's coastal town for her mother's funeral. There, a stranger named Ilse greets the mourners using the family's true surname, a name Wendell has never heard, and claims to have letters proving her mother lived an entire life before the one Wendell knew. As Wendell translates the letters—written partly in the dialect she is forgetting word by word—she uncovers that her father was not who she believed, and that her mother chose silence over truth to protect her. The climax comes when Wendell must decide whether to read aloud at the estate reading the final letter, which names her real parentage, or burn it as her mother asked; she reads it, shattering the family myth but finally claiming her own name. In the end, Wendell stays in the town, teaching the dialect to Ilse's granddaughter, becoming an owner of her history rather than its tenant.
about_author: Petra Voss is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent fifteen years translating testimony in immigration hearings before turning to fiction. She writes about language, exile, and the families we invent to survive our real ones.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Wendell's POV. Wendell returns to Greyharbor for her mother Marguerite's funeral, staying in the shuttered family house like a guest. She notices a dialect word slipping from her memory on the train. Emotional beat: numb displacement, grief deferred behind professional detachment.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the wake, the stranger Ilse Vantol addresses the family as 'the Alderinks,' a surname no one recognizes. Wendell's uncle silences Ilse sharply; her aunt's hands tremble. Wendell pretends not to hear. Emotional beat: first crack in the known world—the reader feels the floor tilt with her.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, flashback braided with present. She recalls how her mother rationed the dialect at home, translating only weather and recipes, never feelings. Now she tests herself against an old children's prayer and finds gaps where words used to live. Emotional beat: quiet dread of losing the key before finding the lock.

chapters.title: Ilse
chapters.summary: Wendell tracks Ilse to a boarding house by the seawall. Ilse reveals she was Marguerite's childhood friend—and that Marguerite wrote to her for forty years, letters Ilse has kept but never opened since the quarrel that ended them. Emotional beat: wary alliance; two women circling the same silence.

chapters.title: The Letters Begin
chapters.summary: Wendell begins translating the letters, working slowly because the dialect fails her. The early letters describe a girl named Marguerite Alderink who loved someone forbidden—a married man named Cor, or so it seems. Emotional beat: intoxication of discovery shadowed by guilt at reading her mother's private voice.

chapters.title: What the Uncle Knew
chapters.summary: Uncle Pieter confronts Wendell, demanding she stop; he burns two letters in the kitchen sink. His fury reveals he has always known something. Wendell realizes the family's loyalty was purchased with her ignorance. Emotional beat: betrayal hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Cor
chapters.summary: Wendell finds Cor Alderink's grave in the churchyard—dated the year before her birth—and then finds Cor's living brother, who confirms Cor was Wendell's father. The middle letters, reread, were never about a love affair but about a rape the family buried. Emotional beat: devastation; identity collapses and reassembles around a harder truth.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Wendell dreams in full dialect for the first time in decades—her mother young, planting a glasshouse, whispering the sentence Wendell cannot yet translate. She understands the language wasn't lost but locked away deliberately, word by word, by her mother's choices and her own obedience. Emotional beat: grief transmuting into clarity.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: In the final letter, Marguerite asks Wendell either to speak the truth at the estate reading or to burn everything. The closing sentence resists translation—it means both 'I protected you' and 'I imprisoned you.' At the reading, with the whole town present, Wendell chooses to read it aloud in dialect, then translate it herself, naming Cor publicly. Emotional beat: climax—costly, liberating speech.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: Weeks later. The family fractures but does not shatter; Pieter leaves without forgiveness, her aunt stays. Wendell takes rooms above the boarding house and begins teaching the dialect to Ilse's granddaughter, recovering words together. She signs a new document—her name, both names. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging earned through truth rather than silence.
